draft.title: The end of the Viking age
card: The Viking age is usually dated from the raid on Lindisfarne in 793 to the middle of the 1000s. It did not end in a single day.
Scandinavian kingdoms grew stronger. Kings gained more control over their lands and their warriors.
These kingdoms also became Christian. Christian kings were less likely to back raids on Christian lands, and raiding faded.
The Viking king Harald Hardrada was defeated at Stamford Bridge in England in 1066. Historians often take this defeat as the end of the Viking age.
draft.remember: Raiding faded as kings grew stronger and Christian, and 1066 is a convenient end date.

a.q: Which change in Scandinavia helped raiding to fade?
opts: Kingdoms grew stronger and became Christian
Farmland became so plentiful that trade stopped
Longships could no longer cross the ocean
Settlers in Iceland took over the Scandinavian kingdoms
a.why: Stronger kings controlled their warriors, and Christian kings were less likely to back raids on Christian lands. Longships were still sailed, and the card gives no sign that farmland or trade ended raiding.
a.clue: Think about who ruled Scandinavia and what they believed.

b.q: Why do historians say 1066 is only a convenient end date for the Viking age?
opts: Raiding had been fading for years before the defeat
Viking raids carried on at full strength after 1066
Stamford Bridge was the first Viking defeat in England
Scandinavian kingdoms became Christian only in 1066
b.why: Raiding faded gradually as kingdoms grew stronger and became Christian, so the age did not end in one day. Stamford Bridge is a handy marker, but it did not cause the change and was not the cause of the kingdoms becoming Christian.
b.clue: Did the Viking age end in a single day?

a.best: Kingdoms grew stronger and became Christian

b.best: Raiding had been fading for years before the defeat

problems.detail: The question says historians call 1066 'only a convenient end date', but the card never uses 'convenient'. proposal.title: The end of the Viking age
card: The Viking age is usually dated from the raid on Lindisfarne in 793 to the middle of the 1000s. It did not end in a single day.
Scandinavian kingdoms grew stronger. Kings gained more control over their lands and their warriors.
Over the 900s and 1000s, these kingdoms also became Christian. Christian kings were less likely to back raids on Christian lands, so raiding faded over many years.
The Viking king Harald Hardrada was defeated at Stamford Bridge in England in 1066. Historians often take this defeat as the end of the Viking age.
proposal.remember: Raiding faded slowly as kings grew stronger and Christian. The defeat in 1066 is often taken as the end.

a.q: Which change in Scandinavia helped raiding to fade?
opts: Kingdoms grew stronger and became Christian
Kings lost control over their lands and warriors
Kingdoms turned away from Christianity
Kingdoms split into many weak chiefdoms
a.why: Stronger kings controlled their warriors, and Christian kings were less likely to back raids on Christian lands. Losing control or turning away from Christianity is the reverse of what happened.
a.clue: Think about who ruled Scandinavia and what they believed.

b.q: Historians often take the defeat at Stamford Bridge as the end of the Viking age. Why did the age not end in a single day?
opts: Raiding had been fading for years before the defeat
Viking raids carried on at full strength after 1066
Harald Hardrada won the battle at Stamford Bridge
Scandinavian kingdoms became Christian only in 1066
b.why: Raiding faded over many years as kingdoms grew stronger and became Christian, so 1066 marks the end rather than causing it. The kingdoms became Christian across the 900s and 1000s, not all in 1066.
b.clue: When did the kingdoms start to change?
